Prealgebra · Lesson 11.4

Measuring Segments

Solve this lesson →All lessons

You have spent three lessons on angles, which measure the turn at a corner. Sides are the other half of a shape. A segment is the straight path between two points, and its length is the distance from one end to the other. Over the next few lessons you will split a segment into pieces, add those pieces back together, and add up all the sides of a shape to find the distance around it.

Problem
In the diagram above, MM is the midpoint of ABAB and the tick marks show the two halves are equal. Given AM=7AM=7, find ABAB. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • A midpoint splits a segment into two equal pieces, so MBMB has the same length as AMAM.
  • The whole ABAB is those two equal halves added together. Double the 77.
Show the full solution
The midpoint MM cuts ABAB into two equal halves, so MB=AM=7MB=AM=7. The whole segment is both halves together, which means AB=2×7AB=2×7. So AB=14AB=14​.
Problem
In the diagram above, MM is the midpoint of ABAB with AB=24AB=24, and NN is the midpoint of MBMB. Find ANAN. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • Start with MM. A midpoint splits the whole into two equal halves, so what does that make AMAM and MBMB?
  • Now NN sits in the middle of MBMB, which gives you MNMN. Then ANAN is AMAM and MNMN added together.
Show the full solution
Since MM is the midpoint of ABAB, AM=MB=12AM=MB=12. Then NN is the midpoint of MBMB, so MN=6MN=6. Going from AA to NN covers AMAM then MNMN, so AN=AM+MN=12+6=18.AN=AM+MN=12+6=18​. Each midpoint only halves the segment it belongs to, so NN cuts MBMB in half, not ABAB.
Key idea
Segments, length, and the midpoint. A segment is the straight path between two endpoints, and we name it by its endpoints, like segment ABAB. Its length is the distance between them, written just ABAB with the units dropped, so AB=12AB=12 means twelve units long. The midpoint is the point exactly halfway between the endpoints, and it splits the segment into two equal parts. If MM is the midpoint of ABAB, then AM=MB=12ABAM=MB=21​AB, and AB=2 AMAB=2AM. Matching tick marks on the two parts mean they are equal, so you can read AM=MBAM=MB off the diagram without measuring.
Problem
In the diagram above, BB lies on ACAC with AB=8AB=8, and the bracket shows the whole segment AC=20AC=20. Find BCBC. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • The two pieces ABAB and BCBC together make up the whole segment ACAC, so AB+BC=ACAB+BC=AC.
  • Put in the lengths you know and subtract to solve for BCBC.
Show the full solution
The two pieces ABAB and BCBC add up to the whole, so AB+BC=ACAB+BC=AC. That reads 8+BC=208+BC=20, which gives BC=20−8=12.BC=20−8=12​. Whenever a point sits between the two ends, a missing piece is the whole minus the piece you know.
Problem
In the diagram above, ABAB, BCBC, and CDCD each carry one tick mark, so the three pieces are equal, and AD=27AD=27. Find the length of ABAB. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • The tick marks tell you ABAB, BCBC, and CDCD are all the same length, and together they make up ADAD.
  • Three equal pieces fill AD=27AD=27, so split that whole into three.
Show the full solution
The tick marks mean ABAB, BCBC, and CDCD are equal, and end to end they make up AD=27AD=27. So each piece is 27÷3=9.27÷3=9​.
Key idea
Segment addition and congruent segments. When a point BB lies on segment ACAC between the ends, the two pieces add to the whole. AB+BC=ACAB+BC=AC Add two known lengths to get the total, or subtract a known piece from the whole to get the other piece. If AC=20AC=20 and AB=8AB=8, then BC=20−8=12BC=20−8=12. This is the segment version of angle addition. Segments of equal length are congruent, and segments marked with the same number of ticks are congruent. Equal pieces in a row total one length times the number of pieces, so five pieces of length 33 make 5×3=155×3=15.
Problem
The diagram above shows a rectangle that is 88 units wide and 55 units tall. Find its perimeter. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • The perimeter is the distance all the way around, so add up the lengths of all four sides.
  • A rectangle has two widths and two heights. You can add 8+5+8+58+5+8+5, or take 2×(8+5)2×(8+5).
Show the full solution
A rectangle has two sides of length 88 and two of length 55, so the perimeter is 8+5+8+5=268+5+8+5=26​. A faster route is to add one width and one height, then double, 2×(8+5)=262×(8+5)=26.
Problem
The diagram above shows a regular hexagon. All six sides are equal, marked by the ticks, and its perimeter is 6666. Find the length of one side. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • The perimeter is the sum of all the side lengths. Since the ticks tell you every side is equal, the six equal sides add up to 6666.
  • Six equal sides summing to 6666 means one side is 6666 split into 6 equal parts. Divide to find it.
Show the full solution
A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides, so the perimeter is one side length added six times. To get a single side, split the perimeter into 6 equal parts. 66÷6=1166÷6=11 So one side is 1111​.
Problem
The diagram above shows an L-shaped figure with its six side lengths marked 66, 22, 44, 33, 22, and 55. Find its perimeter. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • The perimeter is the distance all the way around, so it is the sum of every side. An L-shape has six sides, and each one is marked in the diagram.
  • Add all six lengths together in one running total, making sure you use each marked number exactly once.
Show the full solution
The perimeter is the sum of all the sides, so add the six marked lengths. 6+2+4+3+2+5=226+2+4+3+2+5=22 The perimeter is 2222​.
Problem
The diagram above shows an isosceles triangle whose two equal legs, marked with ticks and labelled 2x2x, are each twice its base, labelled xx. The perimeter is 4040. Find the base. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • The perimeter is the sum of all three sides, so add the two legs and the base and set that equal to 4040.
  • The two legs are each 2x2x and the base is xx, so combine the like terms into one xx term before solving.
Show the full solution
The perimeter is the sum of the three sides, so 2x+2x+x=402x+2x+x=40. Combining the like terms gives 5x=405x=40, so x=8x=8. The base is xx, which is 88​.
Key idea
Perimeter. The perimeter of a closed figure is the total distance around it. Add the lengths of all its sides. For a triangle with sides 55, 66, and 77, the perimeter is 5+6+7=185+6+7=18. In a regular polygon every side is equal, so instead of adding side by side, multiply one side by the number of sides. A regular hexagon with side 44 has perimeter 6×4=246×4=24.
Problem
In the diagram above, two sides of a triangle are 77 and 99, and the third side (marked with a question mark) is a whole number. Find the largest the third side could be. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • The third side of a triangle is always shorter than the other two sides added together. Add the two given sides.
  • Once you have that sum, the third side has to be less than it. Since the side is a whole number, take the biggest whole number below that sum.
Show the full solution
The two given sides add to 7+9=167+9=16, and the third side has to come in under that, so the biggest whole number it can be is 1515​. Any side of a triangle is less than the sum of the other two. At exactly 1616 the triangle flattens into a straight line.
Problem
In the diagram above, two sides of a triangle are 77 and 99, and the third side (marked with a question mark) is a whole number. What is the smallest the third side could be? Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • The triangle inequality says any two sides must sum to more than the third. Turn that around. The third side must be more than the difference of the other two.
  • Find 9−79−7, then pick the smallest whole number that is strictly larger than it.
Show the full solution
By the triangle inequality, the third side has to be more than the difference of the other two, or the triangle collapses flat. That difference is 9−7=29−7=2, so the third side must be more than 22. The smallest whole number bigger than 22 is 33​.
Problem
In the diagram above, two sides of a triangle are 44 and 99, and the third side (the question mark) is a whole number. How many different whole-number lengths are possible for it? Give the number of whole-number lengths.
Show a hint
  • The triangle inequality says the third side has to be less than the sum of the other two and more than their difference. Work out both of those bounds from 44 and 99.
  • The third side must be more than 9−49−4 and less than 9+49+4. Count the whole numbers strictly between those two bounds.
Show the full solution
The triangle inequality traps the third side between the sum and the difference of the other two sides. It has to be less than 9+4=139+4=13 and more than 9−4=59−4=5, so 5<third side<13.5<third side<13. The whole numbers strictly between 55 and 1313 are 6,7,8,9,10,11,126,7,8,9,10,11,12. That is 77​ possible lengths.
Key idea
The triangle inequality. Any two sides of a triangle add to more than the third side. So three lengths form a triangle only when the two shorter ones add to more than the longest. If they add to the longest or less, the two shorter sides cannot meet, and there is no triangle. Written the other way, the unknown third side must be less than the sum and more than the difference of the other two.
Fun fact
The word perimeter comes straight from Greek. "Peri" means around and "metron" means measure, so perimeter literally says "measure around". That same "peri" turns up in a periscope, which lets you see around a corner, and in a perimeter fence that runs all the way around a property. Once you spot the "peri", you can hear the meaning hiding inside the word.
Problem
In the diagram above is a triangular garden with sides 1313, 1414, and 1515 feet. Fencing costs $4$4 per foot. Find the total cost to fence it. Give the number of dollars.
Show a hint
  • The fence runs all the way around, so start with the perimeter, the sum of the three sides.
  • Once you have the perimeter in feet, multiply by the cost of a single foot.
Show the full solution
The fence runs the whole border, so start with the perimeter, 13+14+15=4213+14+15=42 feet. Each foot costs $4$4, so the total is 42×4=16842×4=168​ dollars.
Problem
In the diagram above, points BB and CC lie on segment ADAD with ACAC and CDCD in the ratio 3:13:1, and BB is the midpoint of ACAC. The bracket shows BC=6BC=6. Find ADAD. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • Since BB is the midpoint of ACAC, the bracket BC=6BC=6 is exactly half of ACAC. Use that to find the whole of ACAC first.
  • Once you know ACAC, the ratio AC:CD=3:1AC:CD=3:1 tells you CDCD. Then ADAD is just AC+CDAC+CD.
Show the full solution
The midpoint BB splits ACAC into two equal halves, so BCBC is half of ACAC. That gives AC=2×6=12AC=2×6=12. The ratio AC:CD=3:1AC:CD=3:1 means CDCD is a third of ACAC, so CD=12÷3=4CD=12÷3=4. Then AD=AC+CD=12+4=16AD=AC+CD=12+4=16​.

Practice these ideas

Practice
In the diagram above, MM is the midpoint of PQPQ and PM=11PM=11. Find PQPQ. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
The midpoint splits PQPQ into two equal halves, so PQPQ is twice PMPM. PQ=2×11=22PQ=2×11=22​
Practice
In the diagram above, BB lies on ACAC with AB=13AB=13, and the bracket marks the whole length AC=30AC=30. Find BCBC. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
The point BB splits ACAC into two pieces, ABAB and BCBC, that add up to the whole. So BC=AC−ABBC=AC−AB. Reading the diagram, AC=30AC=30 and AB=13AB=13, which gives BC=30−13=17.BC=30−13=17​.
Practice
In the diagram above, the tick marks show that XYXY, YZYZ, ZWZW, and WVWV are all equal, and the whole length XV=32XV=32. Find XYXY. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
The four tick marks mean XYXY, YZYZ, ZWZW, and WVWV are equal pieces that add up to XVXV. So one piece is a quarter of the whole. XY=324=8XY=432​=8​
Practice
In the diagram above, MM is the midpoint of ABAB with AB=20AB=20, and NN is the midpoint of AMAM. Find NBNB. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
Each midpoint cuts a segment in half. Since MM is the midpoint of ABAB, we get AM=202=10AM=220​=10. Since NN is the midpoint of AMAM, we get AN=102=5AN=210​=5. Then NN sits 55 units from AA, so NB=AB−AN=20−5=15.NB=AB−AN=20−5=15​.
Practice
The diagram above shows a rectangle that is 99 wide and 66 tall. Find its perimeter. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
The perimeter is the sum of all four sides. A rectangle has two sides of length 99 and two of length 66, so add one of each and double it. 2×(9+6)=2×15=302×(9+6)=2×15=30 The perimeter is 3030​.
Practice
The diagram above shows an L-shaped figure with its six sides labelled. Find its perimeter. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
The perimeter is the sum of every side, so add the six labelled lengths. 7+2+4+3+3+5=247+2+4+3+3+5=24​
Practice
In the diagram above, the two equal legs of the isosceles triangle each measure 2x2x, the base measures xx, and the perimeter is 3535. Find the base. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
The perimeter is the sum of the three sides, so add the two legs and the base. Each leg is 2x2x and the base is xx, which gives 2x+2x+x=35.2x+2x+x=35. Combine the like terms to get 5x=355x=35, so x=7x=7. The base is xx, so its length is 77​.
Practice
The diagram above shows a regular octagon with perimeter 7272. Since all eight sides are equal, find the length of one side. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
All eight sides of a regular octagon are equal, so one side is the perimeter split into 88 equal parts. 72÷8=972÷8=9 One side has length 99​.
Practice
In the diagram above, two sides of the triangle measure 88 and 1111, and the third side is a whole number. What is the largest length the third side can be? Give the number of units.
Show the solution
By the triangle inequality, the two known sides must sum to more than the third side, so the third side is less than 8+11=198+11=19. The largest whole number below 1919 is 1818​.
Practice
In the diagram above, a triangle has two sides of length 88 and 1111, and its third side is a whole number of units. What is the smallest length that third side can be? Give the number of units.
Show the solution
For a triangle to close up, the third side must be longer than the difference of the other two, so 11−8=311−8=3. The side has to be more than 33, and the smallest whole number that beats 33 is 44​.
Practice
In the diagram above, two sides of a triangle are 66 and 1010, and the third side is a whole number. How many different whole-number lengths could the third side be? Give the number of whole-number lengths.
Show the solution
By the triangle inequality, the third side must be less than the sum of the other two and more than their difference. So it is more than 10−6=410−6=4 and less than 10+6=1610+6=16, giving 4<third<164<third<16. The whole numbers strictly between 44 and 1616 run from 55 to 1515, which is 15−5+1=1115−5+1=11 values. The answer is 1111​.
Practice
The diagram above shows a square garden that measures 1414 feet on each side. Fencing costs $5$5 per foot, and you want to fence the whole garden. How much will the fencing cost? Give the number of dollars.
Show the solution
Fencing follows the border, so start with the perimeter. A square has four equal sides, so the perimeter is 4×14=564×14=56 feet. Each foot costs $5$5, so the fencing costs 56×5=28056×5=280​ dollars.
Practice
In the diagram above, BB and CC lie on segment ADAD with AB:BC:CD=3:4:5AB:BC:CD=3:4:5, and AD=36AD=36. Find BCBC. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
The ratio splits ADAD into 3+4+5=123+4+5=12 equal pieces. So one piece is 36÷12=3.36÷12=3. Now BCBC is worth 44 of those pieces, so BC=4×3=12BC=4×3=12​.
